title: Framework | Memory and storage pricing updates
text:
# Navigating the volatile silicon market: updates on memory and storage pricing

News Nov 06 2026 by Nirav Patel 

 

Updated on November 6th, 2026

We’ve been able to keep DDR5 pricing stable for the last few months by buffering inventory. We’ve now depleted some of our earlier, lower-cost inventory, and as a result are facing cost increases on some module capacities and on pre-built configurations of Framework Laptop 12.

For the DDR5 modules used in our DIY Edition configurators, we’ve needed to increase pricing on 16GB, 32GB, and 48GB capacities. As before, we’re limiting the price increases to cover the increased costs coming from our suppliers. This means that even with these updates, our pricing on 16GB and 32GB modules sits within the range of what we’re currently seeing at retail, and our 48GB pricing remains below it. As always, if you find a better deal elsewhere, you can bring your own memory with a Framework Laptop DIY Edition.

On Framework Laptop 12, we’ve depleted the original lower-cost inventory of pre-built systems with 8GB of DDR5, and have updated the pricing on both the entry-level Linux and Windows pre-built configurations. The remaining pre-built configurations and our DIY Edition system pricing remains unchanged. 

As with previous updates, we’ll continue to honor pricing from order time on existing pre-orders. Note that modifying the memory configuration on an existing pre-order will update that item to the new pricing. We’ll keep you updated as we navigate this environment, and as we’ve committed from the start, we’ll bring prices back down as suppliers bring costs down or as we find alternative sources of lower-cost memory.

Updated on September 29th, 2026

We have another positive update today on LPCAMM2 and Core Ultra X9! We were able to get additional shipments of both under the same pricing as the previous shipment. This means we’ve extended the LPCAMM2 price decrease to all remaining Framework Laptop 13 Pro pre-orders and reduced the memory pricing for new pre-orders too. This means our new pricing for 32GB and 64GB LPCAMM2 for the DIY Edition, and our pre-built X7 configuration that uses 32GB are now at a lower price. The X9 processor is now also open to new pre-orders. Note that for each of these, we have limited quantities. This means that for memory, if we’re unable to source additional memory at this pricing, once we deplete this shipment, we’ll need to increase pricing again for new pre-orders past that point. Similarly for X9, we’ve created new X9-specific limited-quantity pre-order batches. As we’re able to receive additional X9 processors, we’ll create further batches.

Just like with the last LPCAMM2 price update, we’re refunding shipped orders on the price difference, updating pricing on any pending pre-orders, and giving existing DIY Edition pre-order customers the opportunity to adjust their memory configuration at the new pricing.

Alongside this positive update, we have an unfortunate update around pricing on our in-stock pre-built Framework Laptop 13 and Framework Laptop 16 configurations that use DDR5 modules. We’ve depleted inventory of several configurations that we built with lower cost memory and storage, and have now needed to increase pricing. We anticipate needing to increase pricing on additional pre-built configurations over the next months as we deplete the inventory there too.

...

Updated on September 8th, 2026

We have some positive updates today around LPCAMM2 memory availability and Intel Core Ultra X9 processor options for Framework Laptop 13 Pro.

Framework Laptop 13 Pro LPCAMM2 & Core Ultra X9 updates

Following our update in July where supplier cost increases forced us to adjust memory configurations and pricing, our Supply Chain team has been working continuously to source additional inventory at better prices. We have good news: we recently secured a limited quantity of Micron 32GB and 64GB LPCAMM2 memory modules at lower cost.

We are committed to passing on savings whenever we can and keeping computers as accessible as possible in the current environment, so we are rolling out price reductions across both already shipped and a subset of currently pending pre-orders. While these new costs remain above our original pre-order launch baseline, they are lower than the last cost update that drove our current pricing for new pre-orders.

On the Core Ultra X9, we had a very limited quantity when we opened pre-orders of Framework Laptop 13 Pro, and we sold out of them almost immediately. We’ve been working with Intel for the last several months and have finally gotten allocation of an additional limited quantity of X9 processors. With that, we’re opening up a new pre-order batch, first to a subset of currently pending pre-order customers. Note that this new processor inventory unfortunately came at a higher cost than our original launch batch, and we’ve had to increase pricing as a result. The new X9 batch ships this November.

Updates for existing pre-order customers

Because we have limited quantities of both the lower cost memory inventory and the X9 processors on hand, we are rolling out access starting with existing pre-order customers up to Batch 10. If we have additional inventory left after this or are able to source additional lower-cost memory or X9 processors, we will then open these to remaining pre-order batches, and then finally to new pre-orders.

- Refunds for shipped orders: If your order has already shipped and you were charged the higher price for LPCAMM2 memory, we are automatically issuing a refund for the price difference down to this lower pricing.
- Price reductions for pending pre-orders: For pending pre-orders through Batch 10 that have memory configured at the higher pricing, we are automatically adjusting to the lower price.
- Order modifications for pending pre-order customers: For pending pre-order customers up through Batch 10 who wish to adjust their memory configuration, we are opening up the option to edit the pre-order to 32GB or 64GB LPCAMM2 at this reduced pricing. Additionally, we are offering pending pre-order customers through Batch 10 first access to upgrade and enter the Intel Core Ultra X9 processor batch. This can be completed on the Order Summary page. More information about modifying a pre-order can be found here. 
- Order modifications for shipped DIY Edition orders: For customers whose DIY Edition orders have already shipped who would like to switch to 32GB or 64GB LPCAMM2 at the reduced pricing, they have the option to reach out using this dedicated contact form. Our support team will help process the order and provide free return shipping for the original LPCAMM2 module.

...

Updated on July 22nd, 2026

...

After evaluating a number of possible paths forward, we’re proceeding on the one that we believe minimizes the impact of this challenge. We have enough 64GB modules in inventory to cover pre-order batches through Batch 4 of laptops and Batch 7 of Mainboards. For orders beyond that configured with 64GB, we’ve updated the order configuration to use a 32GB module at the original 32GB module price. After that, we allocated the remaining 32GB modules to DIY Edition and Mainboard pre-orders configured with 32GB through Batch 4 of laptops and Batch 7 of Mainboards. For DIY Edition and Mainboard orders beyond that configured with 32GB, we’ve updated the order configuration to use a 16GB module at the original 16GB price. Note that because we don’t currently have a Core X7 Ultra pre-built configuration with 16GB of memory, we have not adjusted pre-built orders that originally contained 32GB. That is a configuration we plan to introduce later.

Alongside these changes to existing pre-order configurations, we’ve updated the pricing on our website for newly placed pre-orders. Our new LPCAMM2 pricing is below the substantially higher cost we’re now sourcing it at to try to mitigate some of the impact to new customers. While we have kept our original 16GB LPCAMM2 pricing for now, we anticipate we will consume the remaining inventory of modules we brought in at lower cost soon, and will then need to increase pricing for new orders. The system and Mainboard pricing for new orders also reflects an upcoming increase in Core Ultra Series 3 processor pricing that impacts X7 and X9 configurations, an increase in Windows license costs, and increases in memory, storage, and other silicon costs for some of our Ryzen AI 300 Series configurations.

...

We're keeping to a roughly monthly cadence on these updates, and unfortunately the trend continues in the direction we expected from last month. Today, we have updated our DDR5 memory pricing for all capacities, now ranging from $12-$16/GB depending on the capacity. As before, we’re selling memory modules for as close as we can to the weighted average cost of our purchases from suppliers. That means in some cases the pricing is slightly below what is available in market. In other cases, there are still retail parts available at lower prices, and we recommend that you pick those up elsewhere alongside your Framework Laptop DIY Edition. We have been able to hold our pre-built system pricing and storage module pricing flat for this month, but we do anticipate increases in the future. We are currently selling some SSD capacities like 8TB for substantially below the available market pricing.

...

Today, we increased our pricing on the DDR5 memory configurable in Framework Laptop DIY Edition orders by 50% to begin to respond to the substantially higher costs we are facing from suppliers and distributors. The new pricing remains below what is available in the open market. We aren’t changing pricing on any existing pre-orders, and we also are not yet updating pricing on our pre-built laptops or Framework Desktop which come with memory (this makes the 128GB config of Framework Desktop a bargain). As always, we also offer the option to buy a DIY Edition laptop with no memory or storage included, letting you re-use modules you have or find deals where you can.

title: Framework DDR5 pricing rises again as its cheaper memory stock runs out
text:
# Framework DDR5 pricing rises again as its cheaper memory stock runs out

Framework has raised DDR5 prices on 16GB, 32GB and 48GB DIY Edition modules and repriced the entry-level Laptop 12 pre-builts after running out of some lower-cost stock.

By

SFF GEEK staff

9 November 2026, 4:41am

Image: Framework

Framework DDR5 pricing is going up again. In an update posted on November 6, Framework says it has run through some of the lower-cost memory it had been holding, and it has raised prices on several DDR5 capacities along with the entry-level Framework Laptop 12.

The company says it had kept DDR5 pricing stable “for the last few months by buffering inventory.” That buffer has now run out for some parts.

## What’s changing with Framework DDR5 pricing

The update covers two areas:

- DIY Edition memory: DDR5 prices are up on the 16GB, 32GB and 48GB capacities in Framework’s configurators.
- Framework Laptop 12 pre-builts: the entry-level Linux and Windows configurations have been repriced, because Framework has used up its lower-cost stock of pre-built systems with 8GB of DDR5.

The remaining Laptop 12 pre-built configurations and DIY Edition system pricing are unchanged.

Framework’s post doesn’t list the old or new dollar figures, so you’ll need to check the configurator for your region.

Framework says its 16GB and 32GB modules now sit within the range of current retail pricing, while its 48GB modules remain below retail.

...

Existing pre-orders keep the price from when the order was placed. Change the memory configuration on one, though, and that item moves to the new pricing.

DIY Edition buyers can still skip Framework’s memory altogether. The company points people to PCPartPicker’s DDR5 listings and says “if you find a better deal elsewhere, you can bring your own memory.” Our guide to everything you need to build a Framework Laptop from scratch runs through the parts involved.

...

This is the latest in a string of updates Framework has published since late 2025. The per-GB DDR5 figures in those updates went from around US$10 in December 2025 to US$12 to US$16 in February, then US$13 to US$18 in March.

It hasn’t all moved one way. On September 29, Framework lowered LPCAMM2 pricing on 32GB and 64GB for the DIY Edition and the pre-built X7 with 32GB, on limited stock, while raising pre-built Laptop 13 and 16 configurations with DDR5 and warning more pre-built increases were likely.

【Seagate Launches FireCuda Forge Device】

Seagate Technology has launched the new FireCuda Forge drive, representing the first Seagate hard drive powered by the Alkemi intelligent storage platform, combining solid-state drive (SSD) responsiveness and hard disk drive (HDD) capacity in a single drive. FireCuda Forge includes an upgradeable HDD, and users can choose and supply their own NVMe SSD for operational compatibility. The product is available in 8TB and 20TB capacities and can add high-speed caching capability to the high-capacity mechanical hard drive through a user-installed NVMe SSD. Its read performance reaches up to 2,500MB/s and write performance reaches up to 2,000MB/s.

...

【AMD Unveils MEXT Memory Management Solution, Halving DRAM Usage Through AI】

According to reports, AMD released MEXT predictive memory software. It uses AI to manage data placement between DRAM and SSD, temporarily staging less-used data on flash storage and then using AI to predict subsequent demand and move it back to DRAM in advance, reducing the time applications wait for data. Tests of specific agent workloads demonstrated by the company showed that DRAM usage could be halved while still retaining 99% of the performance of an all-DRAM configuration. AMD said MEXT can be paired with dedicated NVMe SSDs and used in on-premises, cloud, virtual machine, and container environments. Existing EPYC servers can also adopt it, allowing customers to increase effective memory capacity or reduce physical DRAM configurations in new systems.

...

CoreWeave reported third-quarter revenue of $3.661 billion, up 168% year-over-year, beating analyst expectations, and raised its full-year 2026 revenue guidance to $13 billion to $13.3 billion. On the earning call, CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator said operating margin jumped to 10% from 5% in the second quarter, reaching the target set at the beginning of the year one quarter ahead of schedule; revenue backlog increased to approximately $133 billion, up 138% year-over-year; and active compute capacity expanded to more than 1.7 gigawatts, double the level at the end of 2025. The company stated that the persistent shortage of computing power has driven up pricing. It has raised prices for all product SKUs by approximately 25% in July, implemented a further 10% price increase at the end of the third quarter, and its prices continued to climb in the fourth quarter. CEO Michael Intrator said the company's compute resources are essentially sold out through 2027, and demand for 2028 far exceeds available capacity by several times.

...

【Raspberry Pi 5 and Compute Module 5 16GB Versions Officially Announced Price Increase Due to Insufficient DRAM Supply】

Raspberry Pi officially announced a price adjustment for some 16GB products. The company said that due to insufficient alternative supply of 16GB DRAM, coupled with continued shortages of other components, it has had to further raise prices for some high-density products. Specifically, the 16GB version of Raspberry Pi 5 is increasing by $80 to $385; the 16GB version of Compute Module 5 is increasing by $40. Products with other specifications remain at their original prices. The company said the memory tightness is a phased issue and looks forward to being able to cancel the price increase plan when memory costs decline again.

title: SK Hynix & Samsung: DRAM Up to 15% Pricier This Winter
text:
- SK Hynix reported record third-quarter 2026 revenue of roughly 104.6 trillion won, up 328% from a year earlier, with an 80% operating margin.
- Samsung Electronics also posted a record quarter with 195.3 trillion won in revenue; its Device Solutions (memory) division grew 15% from the prior quarter to a record level.
- Market researcher TrendForce expects fourth-quarter 2026 contract prices to rise another 10% to 15% for DRAM and 15% to 20% for NAND flash.
- SK Hynix expects the global memory shortage to persist until at least 2030 — with knock-on effects for PC, laptop and SSD prices in the US as well.

...

Market researcher TrendForce forecasts that contract prices for conventional DRAM will climb 10% to 15% quarter over quarter in the fourth quarter of 2026, while NAND flash — the basis of SSDs — is expected to rise 15% to 20%. Contract prices are what chipmakers charge large customers such as laptop and smartphone manufacturers; they feed through to retail prices with a delay.

As early as October 2026, the average fixed price for a mainstream DDR4 8-gigabit PC memory chip hit a record $27.50, up 5.77% from September, according to TrendForce data. NAND flash prices, by contrast, temporarily halted a 21-month streak of increases that same month — prices for the benchmark 128-gigabit chip held steady in October.

AMD's rumored Siren Halo APU could depart from the shared-memory design used in its current Halo products. TechPowerUp reports that Gotou_3rd, posting on X on November 12, claimed the chip would have dedicated GDDR7 graphics memory alongside a separate LPDDR system-memory pool. The report gives no memory capacities, interface widths or launch date. It also says AMD has not confirmed Siren Halo, so the proposed configuration remains a rumor rather than an announced specification. ... A split design would raise a different question for local AI users: how much memory could the GPU access directly? The leak does not answer that. Penguin Solutions has introduced the SMART CXL-8F2W-D4, a CXL add-in card designed to bring DDR4 capacity into AI systems.

Read full story

According to the report, AI-related CPU and DDR5 requirements are increasing demand for capacitors on motherboards and memory modules. TrendForce expects the strongest high-end MLCC shortages in the first two quarters of 2027. Murata expansion is not expected to add operational capacity before 2028. The forecast separates this market from weaker consumer components: lower- and mid-capacitance MLCC spot prices fell about 5% in early October before stabilizing. Notebook ODMs expect fourth-quarter orders to fall 10-15% from a year earlier. For RamTrend, the relevance is an adjacent component constraint in the DDR5 supply chain. Capacitor pricing and memory-chip pricing are distinct, and this report does not quantify a resulting change in DRAM prices.

title: RAM and GPU prices: why they keep rising and when they ease
text:
RAM and GPU prices have climbed all year, and the reason is the same for both: the AI boom is swallowing the world’s memory chips. A 32GB kit of DDR5 memory, the standard choice for a new gaming PC, cost about $100 to $200 a year ago. In late October the cheapest one on Tom’s Hardware’s price tracker cost $447. Nvidia’s top graphics card, the RTX 5090, launched at $1,999 in January 2025. On 8 November US retailers listed it at between about $4,500 and $7,700, when they had it in stock at all, TechRadar found.

This piece explains what is driving the rises, who is gaining from them and what the companies that make memory say about when it might end. The short answer is: not soon. All three of the big memory makers say supply will stay tight through 2027, and most new factories will not add output before 2028.

...

- AI data centres are taking most of the world’s memory output, and chipmakers are moving production to the high-bandwidth memory that AI chips use.
- Contract prices for standard memory chips have risen sharply this year, and TrendForce expects another rise of 10% to 15% in the last three months of 2026.

...

For the fourth quarter, TrendForce expects contract prices for standard DRAM to rise another 10% to 15%, and prices for flash storage to rise 15% to 20%. The increases are getting smaller, it said, partly because the starting point is now so high, partly because buyers have less to spend, and partly because long-term contracts limit how far prices can rise. JP Morgan projects that DRAM prices will be up about 400% by the end of 2026 compared with 2024, Engadget reported.
